etymology: From the Latin Clemens, “merciful,” an elder of the church at Rome in the first century, author of the epistle known as First Clement.
biblical_def: Clement was an elder and overseer of the church at Rome at the close of the first century, named by the early writers among the men who had companied with the apostles. About the year ninety-six he wrote, in the name of the church at Rome, a long and weighty letter to the church at Corinth, which had fallen again into the strife and faction the apostle Paul had once rebuked. The letter is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament, and it breathes the apostolic air: it pleads for peace and order, beseeching that they all speak the same thing and that there be no divisions among them (1Co 1:10); it sets forth the resurrection of the dead; and it confesses that the saints are not justified by themselves, nor by their own works, but through faith, by which Almighty God hath justified all men from the beginning. The dictionary honours Clement as an early and faithful witness to the gospel of grace, to the resurrection, and to the godly order of Christ’s church, who called a divided people back to humility and submission one to another (1Pe 5:5). His letter shows a Rome still governed, as the New Testament shows it, by a plurality of elders, not by a single monarch’s throne.
webster_summary: An elder of the first-century church at Rome whose letter to Corinth is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament.
webster_full: CLEMENT OF ROME, an elder and overseer of the church at Rome about A.D. 96.
He was reckoned among the men who had companied with the apostles.
He wrote First Clement to the Corinthians, rebuking their renewed faction.
The letter confesses justification through faith and the resurrection of the dead.
It shows the church at Rome still governed by a plurality of elders.
scriptures: Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: His letter has been wrongly pressed into the service of the later papal claims, against its own plain witness to collegial eldership.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption to name is not Clement’s but Rome’s after him. Because he wrote in the name of the Roman church to the Corinthian, the later papacy claimed him as an early monarch-bishop and made his letter a proof of Roman primacy over all the churches. This is a corruption of the record. Clement writes as one elder among elders, urging peace by entreaty and not by command, and his letter knows nothing of a single ruling pontiff. The dictionary receives his witness and rejects the use later made of it.

What is honourable in Clement is his fidelity to the apostolic gospel. He confessed that men are justified by faith and not by their own works, the very truth the Reformation recovered against the accumulated errors of medieval Rome. So the earliest voice of the Roman church, rightly heard, stands not for the papacy but for the gospel of grace, and rebukes the divisions of the saints by calling them to humility, to submission one to another, and to the peace of Christ.
roots_summary: From the Latin for “merciful,” Clement names a first-century Roman elder and the earliest sub-apostolic writer.

The earliest Roman voice confessed justification by faith, not the later papal throne.
Be clothed with humility, for God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble.

etymology: Greek Athenagoras, “assembly-speaker” or “orator,” a Christian philosopher of Athens in the second century.
biblical_def: Athenagoras was a Christian philosopher of Athens in the latter part of the second century, who about the year one hundred and seventy-seven addressed to the emperor Marcus Aurelius a reasoned defence of the faith, called A Plea for the Christians. The heathen slandered the believers as atheists, cannibals, and workers of incest; Athenagoras answered each charge with calm and ordered argument, showing that the Christians worshipped the one true God, the Maker of heaven and earth who dwelleth not in temples made with hands (Act 17:24), and lived lives of a purity that shamed their accusers. He wrote also a treatise On the Resurrection of the Dead, defending the doctrine that the body sown in corruption shall be raised in incorruption (1Co 15:42). The dictionary honours Athenagoras as a model of the apologist who is ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope that is in him, with meekness and fear (1Pe 3:15). He stood before the throne of the world’s greatest power and was not ashamed of the gospel, contending earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints, and answering the world’s railing not with railing but with truth and reasoned witness.
webster_summary: A second-century Athenian philosopher who defended the Christians before Marcus Aurelius and wrote on the resurrection.
webster_full: ATHENAGORAS, a Christian philosopher of Athens in the second century.
He addressed A Plea for the Christians to the emperor Marcus Aurelius.
He answered the slanders of atheism, cannibalism, and incest against believers.
He defended the worship of the one true God and the purity of Christian life.
He wrote a treatise On the Resurrection of the Dead.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: His apologetic stands against the world’s perennial slander of the church; the apologist’s peril is to lean too far upon the philosophy he answers.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Athenagoras confronted was the heathen world’s slander of the saints, which painted the purest of men as monsters of vice. The same spirit lives in every age that hates the church and must first defame it; and the dictionary honours the reasoned, fearless answer Athenagoras returned, the pattern of all faithful apologetic.

Yet the apologist faces a peril of his own, to lean so far upon the philosophy of his hearers that he borrows their categories in place of Scripture’s. Athenagoras kept his footing, grounding his plea in the one God and the resurrection of the body; but the dictionary marks the danger that beset the apologists and undid lesser men, who would meet the wisdom of the world by becoming wise in its way. The faithful answer to the world is not its own philosophy refined, but the truth of God set forth with meekness and fear.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “orator,” Athenagoras names a second-century Athenian defender of the faith.

The world that hates the church will first defame it; answer slander with truth, not railing.
The faithful apologist grounds his plea in God and the resurrection, not in the world’s philosophy.

etymology: Greek Theophilos, “lover of God” or “loved of God,” a bishop of Antioch in the second century.
biblical_def: Theophilus was bishop of Antioch in the latter half of the second century, and the author of three books addressed To Autolycus, a heathen friend who mocked the faith. In them he defended the one living God, the creation of the world out of nothing in the beginning when God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1), the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the resurrection. He is remembered above all as the first writer known to use the word Triad of the Godhead, naming God, His Word, and His Wisdom, and so giving the church an early term for the doctrine that the Lord taught when He bade the apostles baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost (Mat 28:19). The dictionary honours Theophilus as a defender of the truth of Scripture and an early witness to the Trinity. He met the scoffer not with the wisdom of the Greeks but with the testimony of the prophets, holding that all Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine (2Ti 3:16). His witness to the eternal Word, who was with God and was God (Joh 1:1), stands among the seeds from which the great Trinitarian confessions of the church afterward grew.
webster_summary: A second-century bishop of Antioch, defender of Scripture and the first known writer to use “Triad” of God.
webster_full: THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH, a bishop of Antioch in the second century.
He wrote three books To Autolycus, defending the faith to a heathen friend.
He set forth the one God, creation, the inspired Scriptures, and the resurrection.
He is the first writer known to use the word Triad of the Godhead.
His witness stands among the early seeds of the Trinitarian confession.
scriptures: Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
corruption_summary: He answered the scoffer not with Greek wisdom but with the testimony of inspired Scripture and the early confession of the Triad.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Theophilus answered was the cultured contempt of the heathen for the Scriptures, the scoffing of an Autolycus who would not believe what he had not seen. The dictionary honours the bishop’s reply, which rested not upon the wisdom of the Greeks but upon the witness of the prophets and the inspired word of God.

Theophilus is honoured chiefly for his early naming of the Triad, an instance of how the church, taught by Scripture, came to speak with growing precision of the one God in three Persons. The doctrine was not invented by the fathers but confessed by them, drawn from the baptismal charge of Christ and the opening of John’s Gospel. The dictionary receives such early witnesses gladly, while holding, as they did, that the rule of all doctrine is the inspired Scripture and not the speculation of men.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “lover of God,” Theophilus names a second-century bishop of Antioch.

The Triad he named is the one God in three Persons, confessed and not invented by the church.
All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine.

etymology: Greek Meliton, a bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the second century, famed for his homily On the Pascha.
biblical_def: Melito was bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the second century, a man much honoured in his own day for learning and holiness. Two great labours preserve his name. The first is his homily On the Pascha, a rich and soaring meditation upon Christ as the true Passover, who fulfilled the type of the lamb whose blood was the token upon the houses of Israel (Exo 12:13). For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us (1Co 5:7), and Melito traced the whole shadow of the law to its substance in the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world (Joh 1:29). The second is his journey to the Holy Land to settle the books of the Old Testament, leaving the earliest Christian list of the canon of the Hebrew Scriptures. The dictionary honours Melito as a master of biblical typology, who read the Old Testament as the Lord Himself taught it, beginning at Moses and all the prophets to expound in all the scriptures the things concerning Christ (Luk 24:27). His paschal homily is a fountain of that Christ-centred reading of Scripture which the Reformation recovered and the Reformed church has always prized.
webster_summary: A second-century bishop of Sardis, master of paschal typology and witness to the Old Testament canon.
webster_full: MELITO OF SARDIS, a bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the second century.
He was famed for learning and holiness in his own day.
His homily On the Pascha sets forth Christ as the true Passover.
He left the earliest Christian list of the Old Testament canon.
He is honoured as a master of Christ-centred biblical typology.
scriptures: Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:

And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.
Joh 1:29
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: His Christ-centred typology rebukes the modern reading that empties the Old Testament of its witness to the Lamb.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that Melito’s labour rebukes is the modern habit of reading the Old Testament as mere ancient history or national literature, emptied of its witness to Christ. Melito read the Passover as the shadow whose body is the Lamb of God, and the whole law as a tracing of the gospel beforehand. The dictionary honours this typology as the very method the risen Lord taught on the road to Emmaus.

Melito’s witness to the canon is honoured likewise: he travelled to the Holy Land to learn exactly which books the Hebrew Scriptures contained, and left the church an early and faithful list. The dictionary receives this gladly against the looseness of a later age that would add or subtract from the canon at will. What Christ fulfilled, Melito read aright; and the Scripture he numbered is the Scripture the church confesses, every page of it bearing witness to the Lamb that was slain.
roots_summary: From the Greek Meliton, the name marks a second-century bishop of Sardis and paschal theologian.
roots_lines: Melito — Greek Meliton, a bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor.

usage: Like Melito, read the Passover and all the law as a tracing beforehand of the Lamb of God.
Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; the shadow of Exodus finds its body in Him.
Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, the whole Scripture testifies of Christ.

etymology: Greek Papias, a bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor in the early second century, a hearer of the elders who had known the apostles.
biblical_def: Papias was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the early second century, a man who had heard the elders that companied with the apostles, and who gathered their living testimony in five books called An Exposition of the Oracles of the Lord. Of that work only fragments remain, preserved by later writers, but they are of great price, for in them Papias hands down the earliest account of how the Gospels came to be written: that Mark, the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately what Peter preached of the Lord, and that Matthew set in order the oracles in the Hebrew tongue. This testimony confirms what Luke declares, that the things most surely believed were delivered by those which from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word (Luk 1:2), and that the apostles followed not cunningly devised fables but were eyewitnesses of His majesty (2Pe 1:16). The dictionary honours Papias as an early and valuable witness to the origin and trustworthiness of the written Gospels, the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (Mar 1:1). His care to gather the testimony of those who had heard the Lord’s own disciples is a standing rebuke to every later doubt of the Gospels’ apostolic source.
webster_summary: An early second-century bishop of Hierapolis whose fragments preserve the earliest account of the Gospels’ origins.
webster_full: PAPIAS, a bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the early second century.
He had heard the elders who companied with the apostles.
He wrote five books, An Exposition of the Oracles of the Lord.
His fragments preserve the earliest account of how the Gospels were written.
He testifies that Mark interpreted Peter and Matthew wrote the oracles.
scriptures: Luk 1:2
Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word;
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Mar 1:1
The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;
This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true.
corruption_summary: His witness to the Gospels’ apostolic origin rebukes modern doubt; his own millenarian fancies show the need of sober exposition.
corruption_paragraphs: Papias stands against the corruption of modern criticism that severs the Gospels from their apostolic authors and treats them as the late and legendary growth of anonymous communities. Against this Papias testifies, within living memory of the apostles, that Mark wrote from Peter and Matthew set down the oracles. The dictionary honours his witness as a firm early link in the chain that binds the written Gospels to the eyewitnesses of the Lord.

Yet Papias was also given to a gross and earthly millenarianism, picturing the age to come in fancies of fabulous abundance, and the later church judged him a man of small discernment in such things. The dictionary marks this as a warning. A faithful witness to the facts of the gospel may yet stumble where sober exposition fails him; and the fleshly literalism that filled Papias’s hope of the kingdom is the same temper that later fed the carnal kingdom-dreams the Reformed church has always restrained by the spiritual reading of the prophets.
roots_summary: From the Greek Papias, the name marks an early bishop of Hierapolis who preserved the Gospels’ origins.

usage: Like Papias, the church holds the Gospels bound to the eyewitnesses who delivered them.
We have not followed cunningly devised fables, but the testimony of those who saw His majesty.
A true witness to the facts may yet need the restraint of sober and spiritual exposition.

etymology: Greek Hippolytos, “looser of horses,” a learned presbyter and theologian of Rome in the early third century.
biblical_def: Hippolytus was a learned presbyter and theologian of the church at Rome in the early third century, the most prolific Christian writer of his age in the West. His great work, the Refutation of All Heresies, traced the errors of the gnostics and other false teachers to their roots in pagan philosophy, and earnestly contended against the modalism of his day, which confounded the Persons of the Godhead and made the Father suffer on the cross. Against this Hippolytus held fast the distinction of the Persons, that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, beholding the glory of the only begotten of the Father (Joh 1:14), and that the Son had glory with the Father before the world was (Joh 17:5), even as Scripture testifies that there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one (1Jo 5:7). He died a martyr, banished to the mines of Sardinia for the faith. The dictionary honours Hippolytus as a defender of the truth against heresy and a witness unto blood; yet it does not hide that he fell into a grievous schism, setting himself up as a rival bishop against Rome, before he was reconciled at the last. His learning served the truth, but his contention is a warning that zeal against error must not become the parent of division.
webster_summary: A learned third-century Roman presbyter who refuted heresy and died a martyr, though marred by schism.
webster_full: HIPPOLYTUS, a learned presbyter and theologian of Rome in the early third century.
He was the most prolific Christian writer of his age in the West.
His Refutation of All Heresies traced false teaching to pagan philosophy.
He contended against modalism, holding the distinction of the divine Persons.
He died a martyr, banished to the mines for the faith.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Joh 17:5
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.

Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
corruption_summary: He rightly contended against modalism, yet his own schism warns that zeal against error must not breed division.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Hippolytus fought was modalism, the heresy that denied the distinction of the divine Persons and made the Father Himself to suffer in the flesh. Against this he held the Scriptural witness to the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, three Persons in one God. The dictionary honours his defence of the Trinity and his death for the faith.

Yet his life carries a warning the dictionary will not pass over. In his zeal against the laxity of the Roman bishop Callistus, Hippolytus broke from the church and set himself up as a rival bishop, the first such schism at Rome. He was reconciled only at the end, sharing a martyr’s exile with the very office he had opposed. His error shows that a true zeal for sound doctrine may yet be soured into the sin of division, and that the defender of the truth must guard his own spirit, lest the contender against heresy become the author of schism.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “looser of horses,” Hippolytus names a learned third-century Roman theologian and martyr.
roots_lines: Hippolytus — Greek Hippolytos, “looser of horses.”
He was a presbyter and theologian of Rome in the early third century.
He wrote the Refutation of All Heresies against false teaching.
He contended against modalism and for the distinct divine Persons.
He died a martyr but was marred by an earlier schism.
usage: Like Hippolytus against modalism, the church confesses the distinct Persons of the one God.
Zeal against heresy is good, but it must not become the parent of schism.
The defender of the truth must guard his own spirit, lest contention sour into division.

etymology: From the Latin name Novatianus, a learned presbyter of Rome in the third century, author of an orthodox treatise on the Trinity but the founder of a rigorist schism.
biblical_def: Novatian was a learned presbyter of the church at Rome in the middle of the third century, and the first Roman theologian to write in Latin. His treatise On the Trinity is a sound and able defence of the orthodox doctrine of the Godhead, and for this the dictionary gives him his due. But his name is fixed in the memory of the church for a grievous error. When the great persecution had passed, and many who had lapsed under torture sought to return with tears to the communion of the church, Novatian held that the church had no power to receive them, and that the gravely fallen could never again be admitted to the Lord’s table though they repented. Refusing the bishop chosen at Rome, he set himself up as a rival and gathered a sect that bore his name and lasted for centuries. The dictionary names this rigorism as a corruption of the gospel. Scripture commands that a man overtaken in a fault be restored in the spirit of meekness (Gal 6:1), that the penitent be forgiven and comforted lest he be swallowed up of overmuch sorrow (2Co 2:7), and assures that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive (1Jo 1:9). A purity that denies repentance to the fallen is not holiness but cruelty, and unsays the very gospel it pretends to guard.
webster_summary: A third-century Roman presbyter, orthodox on the Trinity but founder of a rigorist schism denying restoration to the lapsed.
webster_full: NOVATIAN, a learned presbyter of Rome in the middle of the third century.
He was the first Roman theologian to write in Latin.
His treatise On the Trinity is a sound defence of orthodoxy.
He denied that the church could restore the gravely lapsed who repented.
He set up a rival bishopric and founded the rigorist Novatian sect.
scriptures: Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
corruption_summary: His rigorism denied the penitent lapsed any return, a cruelty that unsays the gospel of grace it claimed to guard.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Novatianism, the rigorist error that the church has no power to restore the gravely fallen, even when they return in true repentance. Born of a zeal for purity in the wake of persecution, it hardened into a schism that refused the penitent the comfort of the gospel and shut the door that Christ Himself had opened. The dictionary names it plainly as a departure from the grace of God.

Scripture is decisive against it. The spiritual are to restore the one overtaken in a fault; the penitent is to be forgiven and comforted; the Lord bids us forgive until seventy times seven. A holiness that denies repentance to the fallen is no true holiness but a cruelty, and it betrays a low view of the blood of Christ, as though some sins lay beyond its cleansing. Novatian’s sound doctrine of the Trinity could not save a sect founded upon a denial of grace; and his error stands as a warning that purity divorced from mercy becomes itself a corruption of the gospel.
roots_summary: From the Latin Novatianus, the name marks a third-century Roman theologian and the founder of a rigorist schism.
roots_lines: Novatian — Latin Novatianus, a presbyter of Rome.
He flourished in the middle of the third century.
He wrote a sound treatise On the Trinity.
He denied restoration to the gravely lapsed who repented.
He founded the rigorist sect that bore his name.
usage: Like Novatian’s error, a purity that denies repentance to the fallen unsays the gospel of grace.
Restore the one overtaken in a fault in the spirit of meekness, lest he be swallowed of sorrow.
No sin of the penitent lies beyond the cleansing of the blood of Christ.

etymology: Greek Gregorios, “watchful,” with Thaumatourgos, “wonder-worker,” a third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus.
biblical_def: Gregory, surnamed Thaumaturgus, “the wonder-worker,” was bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus in the third century, a pupil of Origen who turned from the law and philosophy to Christ. He composed a clear confession of the Trinity, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost (2Co 13:14), which long served the church of Pontus as a rule of faith. He was a true missionary bishop, and it is said that he found his city with but a handful of believers and left it with but a handful of unbelievers, so mightily did the gospel spread under his labour, turning men from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God (Act 26:18). The dictionary honours Gregory as a missionary of fervent zeal and a faithful confessor of the Triune God. Yet his very surname, “the wonder-worker,” gathered to itself a crop of legendary marvels in the centuries after him, and his life was adorned with tales the sober reader must weigh against the Scripture. The dictionary honours the man and his real labour, while holding, with the apostle, that charity never faileth, but prophecies and tongues and the sign-gifts of the apostolic age shall cease (1Co 13:8), and that the church is built not on wonders but on the word.
webster_summary: A third-century missionary bishop of Pontus and confessor of the Trinity, whose surname gathered later legends.
webster_full: GREGORY THAUMATURGUS, “the wonder-worker,” bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus.
He flourished in the third century and was a pupil of Origen.
He composed a clear and early confession of the Trinity.
He was a fervent missionary who turned his region to Christ.
His surname gathered legendary marvels in the centuries after him.
scriptures: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God; so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ.
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
corruption_summary: His missionary labour and Trinitarian confession are honoured, while the later cult of his wonders is weighed by the word.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Gregory is plain: a fervent missionary who carried the gospel through Pontus and confessed the Triune God in a creed that fed his people for generations. The dictionary honours such labour, by which men were turned from the power of Satan unto God, and gives thanks for the spread of the gospel under his hand.

The corruption to weigh is not in Gregory’s faith but in the legend that gathered about his name. “The wonder-worker” became a magnet for marvellous tales, and the cult of his miracles grew far beyond the sober record. The dictionary, holding the Reformed and cessationist rule, honours the man while it sifts the legend; for the church is built not upon signs and wonders but upon the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself the chief corner stone. The extraordinary gifts that attended the founding of the church have ceased, and the marvels later heaped upon Gregory’s memory are no part of the rule of faith.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “watchful” and “wonder-worker,” the name marks a third-century missionary bishop of Pontus.
roots_lines: Gregory — Greek Gregorios, “watchful.”
Thaumaturgus — Greek Thaumatourgos, “wonder-worker.”
He was bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus in the third century.
He was a pupil of Origen and a confessor of the Trinity.
His surname gathered legendary marvels after his death.
usage: Like Gregory in Pontus, the missionary turns men from the power of Satan unto God.
The church is built not upon signs and wonders but upon the word of God.
Honour the faithful labourer, but weigh every later legend by the Scripture.

etymology: Greek Eusebios, “pious” or “godly,” bishop of Caesarea in the early fourth century, called the father of church history.
biblical_def: Eusebius was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century, and is justly called the father of church history. His Ecclesiastical History gathered the records of the church from the apostles to his own day, preserving for all later ages the testimony of the early writers, the succession of the churches, and above all the accounts of the martyrs who sealed their faith with blood. For this labour the dictionary owes him, as does every student of the early church, a great debt of gratitude. But Eusebius was no clear champion of the truth in the great controversy of his age. When Arius denied the full deity of the Son, Eusebius wavered, leaning to a subordinationism that fell short of the Scriptural confession that the Word was God, that He is before all things and by Him all things consist (Col 1:17), the brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person (Heb 1:3). He subscribed the Nicene Creed only with reluctance, and ever after kept a courtier’s friendship with the powers of the world. The dictionary honours Eusebius as a historian without peer, while naming plainly the doctrinal weakness that kept him from standing with Athanasius for the eternal and equal Godhead of the Son, who said, Before Abraham was, I am (Joh 8:58).
webster_summary: The early fourth-century bishop of Caesarea, father of church history, but a waverer toward Arian subordinationism.
webster_full: EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, the father of church history.
He flourished in the early fourth century under the emperor Constantine.
His Ecclesiastical History preserves the record of the early church and its martyrs.
He wavered in the Arian controversy toward a subordinationist view of the Son.
He subscribed the Nicene Creed only with reluctance.
scriptures: Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Joh 8:58
Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
corruption_summary: His history is of great price, but his subordinationism failed the deity of the Son that Nicaea confessed.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Eusebius is his history, which preserved for the church the testimony of its first three centuries and the precious record of the martyrs. The dictionary honours this labour and uses its fruit, as all later ages must.

The corruption to name is his doctrinal weakness. In the Arian controversy Eusebius leaned toward subordinationism, treating the Son as less than fully and eternally God, and he came to Nicaea’s confession of the Son as one substance with the Father only with a dragging reluctance. Scripture leaves no room for his hesitation: the Word was God, before all things, the brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person, who said of Himself, Before Abraham was, I am. The dictionary honours Eusebius the historian while it refuses Eusebius the half-Arian, and marks how the courtier’s friendship with the throne too often dulls the edge of a man’s confession.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “godly,” Eusebius names the father of church history, a waverer in the Arian controversy.
roots_lines: Eusebius — Greek Eusebios, “pious” or “godly.”
He was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century.
He is called the father of church history.
His Ecclesiastical History preserves the record of the early church.
He wavered toward Arian subordinationism in the great controversy.
usage: Like Eusebius, a man may serve the church greatly in one gift and fail it in another.
The Son is before all things, and by Him all things consist; no subordinationism may stand.
The courtier’s friendship with the throne too often dulls the edge of confession.

etymology: From the Latin Hilarius, “cheerful,” bishop of Poitiers in Gaul in the fourth century, called the Athanasius of the West.
biblical_def: Hilary was bishop of Poitiers in Gaul in the fourth century, and earned the name of the Athanasius of the West for his unbending stand against Arianism when the heresy, backed by the imperial court, had all but overwhelmed the churches. For his confession of the full and equal deity of the Son he was banished into exile in the East, and there he wrote his great work On the Trinity, a sustained defence of the truth that the Lord declared when He said, I and my Father are one (Joh 10:30), and that the apostle taught when he wrote that Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Php 2:6). Hilary held fast that in Christ dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9), and that the believing confession is that of Thomas, My Lord and my God (Joh 20:28). The dictionary honours Hilary as a faithful and suffering champion of the deity of Christ, who counted exile a small price for the truth of the Godhead of the Son. He is a witness that the cause of orthodoxy is often carried, not by the favour of the powerful, but by the constancy of a few who will not bow, though the whole world for a season seems to have turned Arian.
webster_summary: The fourth-century bishop of Poitiers, the Athanasius of the West, exiled for defending the deity of Christ.
webster_full: HILARY OF POITIERS, bishop of Poitiers in Gaul in the fourth century.
He is called the Athanasius of the West for his stand against Arianism.
He was banished into exile in the East for his confession of the Son’s deity.
In exile he wrote his great work On the Trinity.
He held fast the full and equal Godhead of Christ against the imperial court.
scriptures: I and my Father are one.
Php 2:6
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
corruption_summary: He stood against the Arian heresy that denied the Son’s deity, even when the imperial court had turned against the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Hilary withstood was Arianism, the heresy that the Son is a creature and less than fully God. In his day the error had captured emperors and councils, and faithful bishops were few; yet Hilary would not bow, and was banished for it. The dictionary honours his constancy as the very pattern of how the truth is kept in evil times, by men who will not bend though the world for a season seems to have gone over to the lie.

Hilary’s great labour was to set the deity of Christ upon its Scriptural ground: the Son one with the Father, equal with God, the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in Him bodily, confessed by Thomas as Lord and God. The dictionary receives his witness with thankfulness. Where a slight subordinationism colours a phrase here or there in the fathers of his age, the rule is the Scripture Hilary defended; and his life teaches that orthodoxy is preserved not by the favour of princes but by the faithfulness of those who suffer for the truth.
roots_summary: From the Latin for “cheerful,” Hilary names the suffering defender of the Son’s deity in the Western church.
roots_lines: Hilary — Latin Hilarius, “cheerful.”
He was bishop of Poitiers in Gaul in the fourth century.
He is called the Athanasius of the West.
He was exiled for defending the deity of the Son.
In exile he wrote his great work On the Trinity.
usage: Like Hilary in exile, the truth is kept by those who will not bow though the world turns Arian.
I and my Father are one: the Son is equal with God, the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Orthodoxy is preserved not by the favour of princes but by the faithfulness of sufferers.
